Sieve
SIV
noun
From the Old English sife, kin to the Dutch zeef and the German Sieb; a vessel with a meshed or perforated bottom for separating the fine from the coarse, the grain from the chaff and the dirt.

Biblical Definition

A sieve is the separating vessel — a rimmed frame with a meshed bottom, shaken until what is worthless falls through and what is wanted remains. Scripture uses it twice in the prophets and once, most tenderly, in the upper room. Isaiah sets it in the hand of God against the nations: His breath comes as an overflowing stream “to sift the nations with the sieve of vanity” (Isa 30:28), and what is shaken out of the sieve of the proud is nothing at all. Amos turns it upon Israel and turns it to comfort: “I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as corn is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth” (Amo 9:9). The shaking is real — exile, dispersion, the violent agitation of a whole people among the heathen — and yet in all that shaking not one grain is lost. God knows the count of His own. Then in Luke the LORD names the sifter: “Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat” (Luk 22:31). Satan asked leave and was granted it, as with Job; the sieve is in the enemy’s hand but the enemy is on the LORD’s leash. And against that shaking Christ sets not a prohibition but a prayer: “But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not” (Luk 22:32). Peter fell hard; Peter did not fall through. The sieve holds because the Intercessor does.

Webster 1828 Definition

A vessel with a meshed bottom for separating fine from coarse; a strainer or bolter.

SIEVE, a utensil with a bottom of meshed wire or hair, for separating flour from bran or grain from refuse.

From Old English sife, kin to Dutch zeef and German Sieb.

Its office is separation by agitation — the shaking is the whole work.

Amos makes it the figure of Israel’s dispersion with none lost (Amo 9:9).

Isaiah calls God’s judgment on the nations the sieve of vanity (Isa 30:28).

Key Scripture

Amo 9:9 — "For, lo, I will command, and I will sift the house of Israel among all nations, like as corn is sifted in a sieve, yet shall not the least grain fall upon the earth."

Isa 30:28 — "And his breath, as an overflowing stream, shall reach to the midst of the neck, to sift the nations with the sieve of vanity: and there shall be a bridle in the jaws of the people, causing them to err."

Luk 22:31 — "And the Lord said, Simon, Simon, behold, Satan hath desired to have you, that he may sift you as wheat:"

Luk 22:32 — "But I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not: and when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren."

Modern Corruption

The sifting of Peter is quoted to prove that a true believer may be shaken clean out of grace.

expand to see more

Luk 22:31 is a favourite proof text for the Arminian and the revivalist alike: Satan sifts, therefore the saint may be lost. But the verse cannot be read without the one that follows it, and the two together are among the strongest statements of preservation in Scripture. Christ does not say, I have warned thee to hold on; He says, I have prayed for thee, that thy faith fail not. The outcome is settled in the Intercessor’s petition before the sifting begins, and He adds what Peter will do afterward — when thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren — announcing the restoration before the denial. Satan got exactly what he asked for and still lost. A second misuse runs the other way: men now describe their own drift from the faith as a sifting, as though abandoning doctrine were a work of God upon them. Amos and Luke both make sifting the removal of what was never wheat.

The doctrine to recover is the perseverance of the saints, and the peculiar comfort in Amos’s image. God says He will shake His people among all the nations — and He does; the shaking is severe, and the vessel is often in the enemy’s hand — yet not the least grain shall fall upon the earth. Not one. Not the smallest, weakest, most easily lost of them. The sieve is designed to lose the dust; it cannot lose the grain, because the God who commanded the sifting numbered the wheat before He began. So the believer under trial should ask not whether he will survive the shaking but what the shaking is doing: the chaff of self-confidence goes, and Peter, who had boasted at the table, comes out of the sieve a man who can feed sheep.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The separating vessel — it exists to lose the refuse and it cannot lose the grain.

expand to see more

Sieve — Old English sife, kin to German Sieb.

It works by agitation: the shaking is the sifting.

Isaiah: the nations sifted with the sieve of vanity (Isa 30:28).

Amos: Israel sifted among all nations, yet not the least grain lost (Amo 9:9).

Luke: Satan sifts Simon as wheat, and Christ prays that his faith fail not.

Usage

"Not the least grain shall fall: the sieve loses dust, never wheat."

"Satan asked to sift Peter, and Christ answered the request with a prayer."

"A sieve is made to lose things — which is why God chose the figure for preservation."
